11. **Characters, second package: their lives.** "A living pool", with new characters arriving through doors where the routes from beyond the map come in, never appearing from nowhere ("Arrivals come through doors"; the doors are map data, with first-guess traffic until the edge markets exist), each newcomer's origin, reasons, name and backstory drawn as facts ("Who they are"), and heads rising where men lack one: a chief for a large crowd of loose men, a successor in a band, a leader for mutineers, and one among a fallen court's refugees ("A head rises where men lack one"), "Enough people, not enough good ones", "Hiring as a negotiation", quitting out of loyalty, which breaks the contract and is recorded, ongoing costs, and "Where characters keep their gold" (purse, hoard and their costs), and "Lending to kings" with debt tablets as evidence and claims, not entries in the score; and outlaws on the roads and seas: "Turning outlaw", "The way back" and "Pirates and bandits", which work the routes of item 7; and "Characters deal with each other", messages and in-person exchanges between characters in the same place; "The richest characters" extended to hoards; "Gold is a lifeline" in the kings' requests too, so every request that asks a king to give or keep gold says what that gold means to him; "Characters as sellers of news", free characters offering structured reports at a price they set; and the character requests rewritten after "Stakes, not dispositions", each character's starting system prompt giving him wealth as his victory and, from his traits, his strategy for winning it, the strategy chosen by formula and the prompt written once by a model from it ("How the strategy is made"), with a bold or a careful road from each character's appetite for risk ("Bold or careful, one goal"), script characters following the same strategy, with what gold, gifts, honesty and getting caught mean for him (item 4's report proposes the script's dispositions as persona habits: build this instead); reputation from losses abroad, characters who hear that a court loses its people abroad or puts others' to death growing wary of serving or visiting it, coded explicitly for script characters ("Jobs, not wages"); and, once outlaws exist, the Idrimi line in the primer ("Idrimi, the outlaw who became king" under Echoes from the archive). Also the pool's baseline, fees that clear the market, and characters working for themselves when service pays less ("A baseline, not a limit", "Fees clear the market" and "Working for oneself"), which replace the earlier rule that arrivals respond to demand; and loans and hiring between any two parties ("Lending to anyone", "Anyone can hire anyone"); and "Messengers are errands": from here on, a report or letter from abroad needs a carrier, someone hired, a traveller going that way, or the sender himself; and "Bands are a character's soldiers", bands drawn from the loose men of item 10+, with pirates as bands at sea ("Pirates are bands at sea"); natural losses without old age, and personas that describe experience, never an age ("No age in this game"); and the dead ranked below every living character in "The richest characters". Also the scoring change of 21 October 2026 ("Debts are facts; repayment is a choice"): strength and the richest characters count what is held, so the score stops subtracting back pay owed and the characters' ranking stops counting it, with the script kings' benchmarks recorded before and after.

    - **11e. Cities defended by their men, and a fair scoreboard** (added 29 October 2026, answering item 11d's review; next, before item 12's measurements, since it changes how games go and who wins). Item 11d found a city falling in the first season of every game (525 kingdoms fallen in 50 games, against 158 before), and the fragile city-states that survive winning 48 of 50 games against par. Haakon (29 October 2026): "didn't you say the millitary age male population will defend their city when someone storms, or? Is it still that easy to storm?", and "Agreed to all! Implement expertly!" Two causes, each fixed at its cause. First, the men of a city defend its walls. As built, "The people defend their land" counts only where no troop stands, only when an army enters a province, and as a resistance of 0, 1 or 2 whose thresholds (5,000 and 30,000 men) no city-state's men reach. A storm now meets the city's own men of fighting age on its walls beside any garrison, counted by their number as every unit is, as hostile as they are to the attacker, with the walls multiplying the defenders as they price the storm; the countryside's men still resist an army that enters the province, now by their number too rather than in steps ("The people defend their land" under War). So a small walled city is dear to storm and falls to blockade, hunger or a breach, and no capital falls in its first two seasons on most seeds, the builder rules' line for a playable game. The walls stay as the dossier gives them, with no floor invented; the numbers are first guesses, tuned in item 18. Second, each power is ranked against its own starting position. Par as a mean with falls counted as 0 let any survivor of a fragile position win. Instead each power's result is placed among the results its own starting position gets in the script games, a fall counted as the lowest, and the winner is the power whose result ranks highest among its own position's results ("One scoreboard for every power" under Victory). Then the final score blends that performance with the realm's size, both from 0 to 1, a first guess of equal weights (5 percent size since item 11f, from this item's measurement) tuned in item 18 so that every power has about the same chance of first place; every placement counts, so each king's and city-state's request gives the goal in words, to finish as high as it can, and the end and the reports show the score with size and performance beside it (decided 29 October 2026). Measured: at script play, wins spread evenly across the powers and across Great Kings and city-states, within noise, and the benchmarks recorded before and after. **Stop for review.**

Names give way to everything drawn over the land: a name is shown at a zoom step only where it touches no more important name and no badge, army or fleet counter, ship or envoy, its box measured from the rendered text rather than guessed from its letters (as built, `NameLevels` counts only other names, and the capitals' spaced small capitals run wider than its guess, so Babylon and Susa touch). Counters gather by zoom: below the step where a province's tokens fit beside its city, they show as one token per power in that province with its count, opening into the single tokens as the map is zoomed in ("Map on small screens"). A test fails if any shown name overlaps another name or a marker, at 390 pixels and on desktop, at every zoom step, from the opening and from a game in progress. And the newest version is the one played: a new version takes over at once on the start screen, and during a game a small note says a new one is ready and reloads into the same game when tapped, so a player is never shown an old build after an update without being told. Then Haakon's next answers (29 October 2026: "Agreed to all! Implement absolutely everything you said now expertly!"), five more parts on the same files. The map opens close, the whole board the exception (Haakon: "In paradox games you spend most of the time zoomed in on your general region. Couldn't that work here, that zooming out to the full region is more the exception than the rule?"): a seat opens on its own realm and its neighbours, as item 11c made it; god view and watching open on the Levant on a phone, where most powers meet, and on the whole board on a wide screen; every view keeps its zoom and place when left and come back to within a game; and one button shows the whole map and returns. Provinces take the land's own borders: each border between two provinces runs along the real feature between them, a ridge, a river, a desert's edge or a strait, traced in latitude and longitude from the geography dossiers (`docs/history/`) and the Natural Earth data, as Imperator's provinces do, instead of the straight midlines of the Voronoi cells built today (`art.ts`); where no feature lies between two cities, the midline stays, bent to the terrain. Connections do not change with the drawing (they come from the attested roads); where a drawn border and the map's connections disagree, the pull request lists each case for the design session instead of changing either. The map and the rules show the same land, as it was in 1346 (Haakon, 29 October 2026: "Yes, every crossing like this should be included, and such that both the map and the game physics reflect the actual terrain that was at the time."; "Walls and terrain" under War): every traced border is checked against the rules' passes, great rivers and rough ground, and every pass, great river, strait or desert edge that was a real obstacle in the period (named in the sources as a road over mountains, a river crossed by ford or ferry, or a place armies were held) becomes a crossing on its connection, with the dossier it comes from, while a lesser stream or ridge is drawn but not made one; candidates to check include the Orontes, the Jordan, the Zagros edge, the Nile's cataracts and the Khabur. The land is drawn as it was, where it differs from today's (from the geography dossiers): the Gulf's head reaching towards Ur, as item 11c drew it, the bay of Miletus not yet silted, the Euphrates in its old bed by Sippar and Babylon, and the Delta's branches of the Nile. The crossings go into the rules in item 11f, after item 11e, so that two changes to the rules are never measured at once; the drawing goes ahead before it. And the map says at a glance what each crossing does (Haakon, 29 October 2026: "As long as the map makes it readable at a glance where what effect is to be expected."): every crossing and every stretch of rough ground carries a mark of its kind (a pass, a ford or ferry, a strait, a desert's edge, rough ground), each with its row in the legend, and a tap on one says its effect in words: how much longer it makes the journey and in which season, whether winter makes it dangerous, and that it helps a defender who stands. The lands beyond the game are drawn and named as no one's: north-west Anatolia (Wilusa, Masa), Greece and Crete (Ahhiyawa, Keftiu), Libya, Arabia's deserts, the Zagros and the Iranian highlands, and the lands round the Black Sea, each by the period's own name where the sources give one, in the land's plain colour with no power's, so the map never ends at a bare edge; drawing only, with no province or rule (what becomes a power is "What earns a place", under The world). An island that is not a province is no one's, never drawn in a neighbouring province's colour (as built, Lesbos, Chios and Samos took Apasa's; Lesbos, the Lazpa of the Hittite texts, and the islands south of it belong to no power in 1346). And the map keeps its light colours in dark mode, as a museum map and Imperator's do: the panels around it darken, and the map is only slightly dimmed so it does not glare at night. The colours of the powers stay as they are (Egypt's gold, Babylon's lapis and Alashiya's copper carry their meaning; no source gives Hatti, Mitanni or Assyria a colour). And two things Haakon found playing (29 October 2026): "when you click a province, the information thingy that pops up, if you scroll down on it, the X disappears, so you can't easily close it again without scrolling all the way up. Also, the arrows for units show only the province it starts from and ends up in, but not which provinces they pass through. So in Anatolia the arrow goes through desert sometimes." The province card, and every card and sheet like it, keeps its title and its close button pinned at its top however far it is scrolled, and also closes on Escape and by tapping the map outside it. And every arrow, an order being drafted, an order given and a unit on its way, follows the route the unit will really take, along the roads through each province it passes, as a travelling token already does (`route` in `scene.ts`), instead of a single arc from its start to its end (`arc` in `svg-renderer.ts`); a province it passes through shows as a small mark on the line, and a crossing on the way shows its mark. Checked on a 390-pixel phone and on desktop, in light and dark mode, with pictures in the pull request.
